content: A hiccup, also known as a hiccough, is an involuntary spasm of the diaphragm that typically occurs several times per minute. This spasm causes a sudden influx of air into the lungs, which leads to the closure of the epiglottis, producing the characteristic hic sound. Most episodes of hiccups resolve spontaneously without the need for intervention, although various home remedies and, in some cases, medications are used to shorten their duration. The medical term for hiccups is singultus. While many cases arise spontaneously, hiccups are often triggered by specific situations, such as eating too quickly, consuming a cold beverage alongside a hot meal, belching, eating spicy or very hot foods, laughing vigorously, coughing, excessive alcohol consumption, sobbing (which introduces air into the stomach), certain smoking behaviors, or electrolyte imbalances. Hiccups can also result from pressure on the phrenic nerve by anatomical structures, tumors, or kidney disease. Notably, approximately 30% of chemotherapy patients experience singultus as a side effect of treatment, likely due to diaphragmatic irritation. One proposed benefit of hiccups is their potential role in dislodging food that has become stuck in the esophagus or is moving too slowly. When a large piece of food exerts pressure on the phrenic nerve, the hiccup reflex is triggered. This reflex causes the diaphragm to contract, creating a vacuum in the thoracic cavity. This vacuum generates a pressure differential across the food bolus, assisting its movement toward the stomach. While gravity aids this process in humans, it is less effective in quadrupeds and marine vertebrates, whose esophagi are oriented perpendicularly to gravity. The hiccup mechanism may have evolved as an aid to peristalsis in ancestral species, though its current utility in humans appears minimal. Ultrasound studies have shown that fetuses experience hiccups in utero, possibly as a respiratory system exercise or to prevent amniotic fluid from entering the lungs. However, more research is needed to fully understand the origins and purpose of hiccups. A phylogenetic hypothesis suggests that hiccups are an evolutionary remnant of amphibian respiration. Amphibians, such as frogs and toads, gulp air and water using a motor reflex similar to mammalian hiccuping. Supporting this theory, the motor pathways for hiccuping develop early in fetal life, preceding those for normal lung ventilation. This aligns with recapitulation theory, which posits that hiccups are evolutionarily older than advanced lung respiration. Additionally, both hiccups and amphibian gulping are inhibited by elevated carbon dioxide levels and can be stopped by the drug baclofen, indicating shared physiological and evolutionary roots. Another hypothesis, the amniotic/atmospheric hypothesis, proposes that the brain has two distinct respiratory control systems: one for amniotic fluid respiration in the womb and another for air breathing after birth. Since amniotic fluid is more viscous than air, the diaphragm must exert greater effort to inhale it. If the amniotic breathing system becomes dominant postnatally, it may result in forceful inhalation efforts, which the body quickly overrides to prevent damage to the lungs and other organs. This preemptive control creates a cyclic phenomenon, leading to hiccups until the underlying conditions resolve. This theory is supported by the observation that hiccups are more common in premature newborns, whose atmospheric respiratory systems are less developed. Hiccups can also be caused by certain medications, such as dexamethasone and tiagabine. Various home remedies are commonly suggested for hiccups, falling into categories such as relaxation and distraction techniques, swallowing or eating methods, and controlled breathing exercises. While these remedies may be effective for short-lived and minor cases, they are often ineffective for intractable hiccups. One respiratory remedy involves breathing into a sealed bag to induce respiratory acidosis, which increases carbon dioxide levels in the blood, lowers blood pH, and suppresses aberrant nervous impulses. However, this method can be dangerous and should only be attempted with supervision, as it may lead to lightheadedness or loss of consciousness. Another effective technique involves exhaling all air from the lungs, inhaling deeply, and then attempting to inhale even more air in short, powerful puffs until the lungs are completely full. This method may work by displacing a gas bubble irritating a nerve and causing the spasm. Other remedies include startling the person, drinking water upside down, or consuming something sweet or tart. In babies, hiccups are often stopped by the sucking reflex, such as breastfeeding or using a pacifier. Medical treatment for hiccups is typically reserved for severe and persistent cases, known as intractable hiccups. Medications such as haloperidol, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine, and baclofen are used in these cases, though they often require sedative doses that impair normal activities. Persistent hiccups caused by electrolyte imbalances may benefit from drinking a carbonated beverage with added salt to restore potassium-sodium balance. Intranasal vinegar has also been suggested as a method to stimulate the glossopharyngeal nerve and interrupt the hiccup reflex arc. Experimental treatments include vagus nerve stimulation, which involves implanting a device in the upper chest to send rhythmic electrical bursts to the brain via the vagus nerve. This method has shown promise in treating intractable hiccups. In one notable case, digital rectal massage was found to terminate intractable hiccups by stimulating the vagus nerve. Long-term cases of hiccups are rare but have been documented. For example, Charles Osborne experienced hiccups for 68 years, earning a Guinness World Record. Other cases include a teenager who hiccuped for five weeks and a man in Northern Ireland who has had intractable hiccups for five years, requiring multiple surgeries.
